So after viewing the second part of this film (the first part was shockingly unavailible), I am rather up in the air what this silent film was trying to achieve. It seems that most of the car salepeople in this film aren't really doing work to the capacity that management wants. So they put out a spy to check up on the workers. They find out that they're not even TRYING. Instead, they're hanging out at the local soda shop, playing pool, and occasionally hanging out in front of the dealership to bag the first custimer that came along. (Remember, Car salesman went door to door in the olden…

It's rather simple. A simple narrative about a dealership that's not doing well and the book keeper decides to find out why by following the salesmen (remember its 1927 and car salesmen made calls to prospects then). He sees the salesmen slacking, and then the plot switches to the Chevy sales system pitch. The 1927 dealers watching this were supposed to take notice then and use the system to get the sales up. It probably worked back then. Today people have short attention spans and it's more funny than informative.

Interesting look at what might have been.

This Harman and Ising short is very interesting to see what their animation might have been had they stayed on with Warner up until 1950. I think even though Warner was really hurting bad for characters and content for about a year when they left in 1933, letting them go was a wise decision. Without them gone we might not have ever got the work we did from Tex Avery and others. This cartoon is very lack luster and a sad end for such amazing talent. Their Bosko cartoons at Warner, though clearly attempts to cash in on the popularity of Mickey Mouse, were still highly creative and improved more…

Hugh Harman and Rudy Ising, founders of the original Warner Brothers and MGM animation units (in 1930 and 1934 respectively) and creators of Bosko, were out of the theatrical animation game by 1940. In 1941, Hugh Harman founded his own studio to produce commercial, health, safety, and training films, a couple of which are archived here ("Johnny Learns His Manners" and "The March of Progress"). rv: This US government film attempts to justify the unjustifiable---the forced relocation of Japanese-Americans from the West Coast during WWII. It peddles the myth that there were actual security concerns although stating that "most" of the victims were loyal. No mention of why Italian-Americans or those of German descent were not similarly treated. Nor of why those of Japanese descent in Hawaii were not interned. The ugly fact is that West Coast Japanese-Americans were relocated because they could be and the forced disposition of their property could be acquired for a song by white Americans.…

The preconception that All Japanese Cannot Be Trusted So Lets Move Them Away is explored here obviously.. And, while not over the top as "A Challenge To Democracy" it does provide a more persuading arguement about WHY it was done (although I don't agree with it in the slightest). Once again, the Japanese are all too pleased about this novel American ideas and off they go. They seem a bit TOO chipper about this, as this film purports that they were happily willing to give up their jobs, businesses, houses and way of life to be relocated. Suuuuuure.

Funny! You hear the allies utter the same arguments that the Nazi Germany used to intern the Jews, perhaps even somewhat more poorly done, yet the Japanese quote ''''''''''relocation'''''''''' unquote or the Dresden Holocaust, or the indiscriminate massacre of civilians in virtually every Japanese city that was firebombed is almost never brought up! I guess if the Axis had won the war we'd here about the Holocaust only in passing, on a chance Wikipedia article we'd find ourselves reading, or an old propaganda film. The history is truly written by the winner. Of course, while you hear people…
